title: Luo Yonghao's judgment: comedy is the last text category AI will conquer
dek: He polled top-tier large language models on text creation and got consistent answers: stand-up comedy, with its one-liner density—text so tightly packed with jokes—can theoretically be conquered by AI, but will inevitably rank last among all text types. Which means comedy writers will outlive other creators by several years in the age of AI.
why: Most of the two-and-a-half-hour episode is improvised comic banter; the real judgments and methodology on AI concentrate in the final half-hour.
who: Listeners who enjoy Luo Yonghao and stand-up comedy scene gossip, and want to hear how comedy professionals genuinely assess AI's impact on creative work.
skip: The first two hours are fear-game improvisation largely unrelated to AI; skip directly to 2:02:46.

points.h: Excessive fear kept our ancestors alive
points.body: When early humans heard rustling in the grass, those who overestimated danger—treating every sound as a predator—survived; the relaxed ones got eaten. Modern people inherited this hypervigilance; hormonal shifts trigger baseless alarms everywhere. Men especially suffer in silence, feeling emasculated by admitting fear.

points.h: Learning to refuse unreasonable requests is safer than fearing conflict
points.body: A listener was pestered by a street vendor after an open-mic show. Too afraid to refuse, she paid repeatedly—then the vendor chased after her claiming she hadn't paid. Two comedians had to rescue her. One pulled her aside afterward: ‘Next time, refuse.’ She realized that fearing confrontation more than consequences is what puts you in danger.

points.h: You don't have to become outgoing to accept connection
points.body: A guest advised a socially anxious listener: don't force yourself to become social; just muster courage to not reject when others invite you or show affection. He shared his own experience: he used to decline 100% of social advances. He changed only that one thing—and everything got easier. You don't have to rewire your whole life; just practice catching what others throw.

points.h: AI invents legal citations that don't actually exist
points.body: An intellectual property court worker encountered AI-generated briefs that looked airtight at first glance—even lawyers initially found them persuasive. But scrutiny revealed invented case numbers that don't exist, and citations of laws unrelated to the actual case. Most people have no way to catch these fabrications with their own knowledge.

points.h: Cross-verify between three top models to catch AI errors
points.body: For work that cannot afford mistakes, Luo's solution: subscribe to the three or four best models globally. Take the first result and paste it verbatim into the second, third, and fourth—let each search online for latest facts and catch errors. He uses this constantly and hasn't seen an error survive three independent checks. Caveat: only works with the very top tiers, not the budget models.

points.h: Comedy ranks last in what AI will conquer
points.body: When asked about his fear of AI, Luo gave a specific judgment: he's asked top models about text creation and got consistent answers—stand-up comedy, with its densely-packed one-liners, is a problem AI will theoretically solve, but will definitely come last among all text types. So comedians will outlast all other writers. And comedy requires live audience testing; AI can't fake that in the near term.

points.h: Everyone researches AI; he still edits scripts by hand
points.body: He confesses he feels no change from the AI wave—everyone around him is debating and diving deep, while he still edits comedy the stone-age way: no phone calls with comics, no video. He has to show up in person and sit face-to-face for forty-fifty minutes to hash out one script. Recently it's been relentless. He jokes he works like a caveman, and sometimes that dumb method brings odd reassurance.

points.h: AI remembered a shopping suggestion from two years ago
points.body: A listener shared an uncanny experience: two years earlier she'd asked AI for advice on buying a certain product, then didn't purchase. Months later, shopping for the same category, AI unprompted mentioned that old recommendation was actually superior, now discontinued, and suggested finding it secondhand—better than anything new on the market. She'd completely forgotten the conversation; checking chat history confirmed every word. She found unopened items listed on the secondhand platform.

facts.k: AI-generated news coverage in short-form video

quotes.text: So I asked her, I was asking her, I said, ‘Baby, which floor are you going to?’ Nobody spoke. I don't know why nobody spoke. My classmate wasn't speaking either.

Then Doubao (豆包) gives you an answer that looks really logical. Sometimes what people upload makes even us lawyers think, ‘Hmm, that's actually got some merit.’ But when you look closer, you find things in there like ‘case number 12345’—which doesn't exist at all.

Get subscriptions to the three or four best models. When you're doing serious work, take what the first one outputs, paste the whole thing into the second, third, and fourth ones, and let them find errors.

Comedy is the last text genre that will be conquered. I've asked several of the top models about this, and they all reached the same conclusion: comedy text creation—especially stand-up, with one punchline per line, that high-density writing style—is something AI will theoretically eventually overcome, but will definitely rank last. Which means comedians in the AI age will have several more years to live.
My work is like a caveman's. Like a cook over a wok. Right now if a comic's script needs revision, I have to discuss how to fix it—I can't even call or video chat. I have to physically go there.

So I think if you haven't experienced that flow state with AI, that feeling of it communicating with you from the soul level—if you haven't gotten that feeling, then you're probably either not using it right, or not using it enough.

Even people working in AI globally right now—one hand fear, the other excitement. It points to this: you get joy, happiness, that deep satisfaction of solving unknowns from this work. But there's a shadow hanging over it—it might wipe out humanity. Both are coexisting now.
